title: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n)
excerpt: The patience-sorting solution to LIS: why the tails array works, why its contents are not the answer, and how binary search replaces the quadratic scan.
seoTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n) — Explained
seoDescription: A full walkthrough of the O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence algorithm: the tails array, why binary search applies, and the classic off-by-one that breaks it.

content.text: Given an array, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence — a set of values that appear in order, though not necessarily next to each other. In
the answer is 4, from

The quadratic solution is the one most people reach first, and it is correct. This page is about the one that is not obvious: an O(n log n) method that maintains an array whose contents are, at almost every step, not a subsequence of the input at all — and whose length is nevertheless always the right answer.

The O(n²) dynamic program asks "what is the longest run ending here?" and rescans everything before it. The faster method inverts the question to "for each length, what is the smallest value a run of that length can end on?" That array is sorted by construction, so binary search applies, and its length is the answer even though its contents usually are not.

body.text: Why the obvious dynamic program is too slow

content.text: Let

i

j

This is easy to justify and easy to get right. It is also two nested loops, and at 100,000 elements that is ten billion comparisons. The judge's time limit exists precisely to rule it out.

body.text: The idea: track the best ending value per length

content.text: Turn the question around. Instead of asking how long a run ending at each
position
can be, ask: for each possible
length
, what is the smallest value that a run of that length could end on?
Call that array
tails
, so
tails[k]
is the smallest value any increasing subsequence of length
ends with.
Two properties fall out, and everything else depends on them:

Its length is always the answer so far. Position

a sorted array is searchable in logarithmic time. That single fact is what removes the inner loop.

items.text: If there is no such entry, every run can be extended by x, so append it and the longest length grows by one.
If there is one, overwrite it with x. A run of that length can now end on something smaller, which can only make future extensions easier.

body.text: Why it is O(n log n)

content.text: Each of the n values is handled once. The work per value is a binary search over
tails
, which never holds more than n entries, so each search is O(log n). Appending and overwriting are both O(1). That gives O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The quadratic version does O(n) work per element instead of O(log n). At n = 100,000 that is the difference between roughly 1.7 million operations and 10 billion.

items.text: Using upper bound instead of lower bound. That accepts equal values as extensions and silently solves the non-decreasing problem. [7, 7, 7, 7] should answer 1, not 4 — it is the fastest way to catch this.
Returning the contents of tails as the subsequence. The length is always right; the array usually is not a real subsequence.
Appending when the search lands on the last index. Appending is only correct when the index is past the end, meaning no existing entry was large enough.
Forgetting the empty input. An empty array has length 0, and tails is naturally empty, so the base case needs no special handling — but the quadratic version's max() call does.
